## Abstract

## Introduction

The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has enabled the development of sophisticated code agents—autonomous systems that can understand, generate, and execute code across diverse programming environments. These agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in tasks ranging from code completion to full-stack application development, significantly accelerating software development workflows. However, as code agents become more capable and are integrated into critical systems, concerns about their trustworthiness, security, and reliability have intensified.

Code agents differ from traditional code generation tools in their ability to interact with execution environments, make decisions based on runtime feedback, and iteratively refine their solutions. While these capabilities are powerful, they also introduce new attack surfaces and failure modes. A compromised code agent could potentially execute malicious commands, generate security vulnerabilities, or inadvertently access sensitive data.

Red-teaming—the process of systematically probing systems to identify vulnerabilities—has emerged as a crucial methodology for evaluating code agents. Specialized red-teaming agents can simulate adversarial behavior, testing code agents against a variety of attack vectors including prompt injection, jailbreaking, and exploit generation. Understanding both the capabilities of code agents and the effectiveness of red-teaming methodologies is essential for developing safer AI systems.

This paper provides a comprehensive review of research advances in code agents and red-teaming. Our goal is to synthesize knowledge from multiple domains—including deep learning, natural language processing, and cybersecurity—to provide a holistic perspective on this rapidly evolving field.

## Related Work

### Code Agent Architectures

Modern code agents build upon foundational neural network architectures that have revolutionized deep learning. The Transformer architecture [1], which replaced recurrence and convolution with attention mechanisms, has become the backbone of most modern language models. For visual components often incorporated in code agents that process diagrams or user interfaces, residual learning frameworks [2] have proven essential for training very deep networks effectively.

Recent work has extended these foundations to create specialized code agents. Building on the general-purpose capabilities of LLMs, researchers have developed architectures that combine code understanding with execution environments, enabling agents to write, test, and debug code autonomously. These systems leverage both the sequential processing capabilities of Transformers and the feature extraction strengths of residual networks to handle complex code generation tasks.

### Trustworthiness Assessment of LLMs

Evaluating the trustworthiness of LLMs is a prerequisite for understanding code agent safety. DecodingTrust [3] provides a comprehensive assessment of GPT models across multiple trustworthiness dimensions including bias, toxicity, misinformation, and vulnerability to adversarial attacks. This work established standardized evaluation benchmarks that have been adopted by the broader research community.

The findings from DecodingTrust demonstrate that even state-of-the-art models exhibit significant vulnerabilities when subjected to systematic testing. These vulnerabilities are particularly concerning when deployed in code agents, which may be given permissions to execute generated code. The evaluation framework introduced in [3] has been adapted for code-specific assessments, though additional metrics are needed to capture code-related risks.

The framework systematically explores attack surfaces specific to code execution environments, including command injection, file system access manipulation, and network attack vectors.

The work highlights the need for specialized red-teaming methodologies that understand the unique risk profiles of code agents, as generic NLP red-teaming techniques are insufficient for evaluating code execution risks.

### Integration and Future Directions

The intersection of these research areas reveals important opportunities for advancing code agent security. Combining the trustworthiness evaluation frameworks of [3] with the automated attack generation capabilities of [4], and building upon the architectural advances of [1] and [2], could lead to more robust code agent systems. Future work should focus on developing standardized benchmarks for code agent security, improving red-teaming automation, and creating defensive mechanisms that protect code agents without sacrificing their functionality.

Code agents represent a powerful paradigm for automated software development, but their increasing capabilities also introduce significant security and trustworthiness challenges. This paper has reviewed key advances in the field, including foundational deep learning architectures [1, 2], comprehensive trustworthiness assessment methodologies [3], and specialized red-teaming frameworks for code agents [4].

Our analysis reveals that while significant progress has been made, substantial challenges remain. Current code agents exhibit vulnerabilities across multiple attack vectors, and existing red-teaming methodologies are not yet comprehensive enough to ensure robust safety. The specialized nature of code agent attack surfaces—particularly those involving code execution—demands continued research into domain-specific evaluation methodologies.

Future work should prioritize the development of standardized security benchmarks for code agents, the creation of more sophisticated red-teaming agents capable of discovering novel attack vectors, and the design of defensive mechanisms that can protect code agents in real-world deployment scenarios. By building on the foundations established by prior work in deep learning [1, 2], trustworthiness assessment [3], and automatic red-teaming [4], the research community can advance toward code agent systems that are both powerful and trustworthy.
